lead: A form is how a web page asks the user for something and sends the answer to a server. HTTP can carry only text, so the browser flattens a form into pairs of name=value, joins them with &, and ships them either in the URL (GET) or in the request body (POST). Search boxes, login pages, IRCTC ticket booking, UPI payment details and feedback forms all run on this one mechanism. Learn the form element, the controls inside it, and the attributes that label, limit and check the input, and you can build any of them.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.1 for elements and attributes, Chapter 2.2 for nesting and inline text, and Unit 1 for URLs and HTTP methods.

sections.h3: The form element: typing becomes name=value pairs

blocks.text: A form is a container for controls plus instructions for sending them. Two attributes carry the instructions. action is the URL of the server program that will receive the data. method is the HTTP method used, get or post. Leave action out and the browser submits to the current page's URL; leave method out and it uses get.

Each control has a name and holds a current value. At submission the browser walks the controls in document order and builds one name=value pair per control. A control with no name is skipped silently, even if the user filled it.

items: The user clicks a submit button, or presses Enter inside a single-line text field.
The browser runs its built-in validation and blocks the send if a field fails.
It reads the current value of every named control.
With get the pairs are appended to the action URL after a ?; with post they go into the request body.
The browser requests that URL and shows the response in place of the page.

blocks.text: Values are URL-encoded before travel. A space becomes %20 or +, and any character outside plain ASCII becomes a percent sign plus two hex digits, so a rupee sign or a Tamil letter still arrives intact.

GET reads, POST writes. GET keeps the pairs in the address bar: bookmarkable, shareable, limited to a few thousand characters, and wrong for passwords. POST hides them in the body, has no small length limit, and is required for file uploads, where the form also needs enctype="multipart/form-data".

sections.h3: Controls: input types, textarea, select, datalist, button

blocks.text: input is an empty element. Its type changes what the user sees and which on-screen keyboard a phone shows; the pair it sends has the same shape whatever the type.

items: Text family: text, password (dots on screen, plain text on the wire), email, url, tel, search.
Numbers and dates: number, range (a slider), date, all obeying min, max and step.
Colour: color, which sends a value like #1a73e8.
Choice: radio for one of many — radios sharing one name form a group and the chosen one sends its value; checkbox for many of many, each ticked box sending its own value.
Other: file opens the system picker; hidden carries a value the user never sees, such as a record id.
Actions: submit sends the form; reset restores every control to its default.

blocks.text: textarea is the multi-line box. rows and cols size it, and its starting text sits between the tags, not in a value attribute.

select holds option elements. An option's value attribute is what is sent; the text between its tags is what the user reads, and the two may differ. selected marks the default option. optgroup with a label groups related options under a heading, and multiple on the select allows more than one choice.

datalist attaches suggestions to a text input through list="id": the user may pick one or type something else, and whatever is in the box is sent. A button element is a submit button that may hold HTML, with type="submit", "reset" or "button".

sections.h3: Labels, groups and the attributes that check input

blocks.text: A label with for="x" is tied to the control whose id is x. Clicking the label focuses the control, and a screen reader announces the label with the field. Labels matter most for radios and checkboxes, where a tiny square is hard to hit on a phone.

fieldset draws a box around related controls and legend gives it a caption. A radio group belongs in a fieldset so the question and its options travel together; disabling the fieldset disables every control inside it.

items: name — the key in the pair; no name means no data.
value — the value sent when the user changes nothing.
placeholder — grey hint text inside the box; never submitted.
required — the form cannot be sent while the field is empty.
readonly — visible, not editable, still submitted; disabled — greyed out and not submitted.
pattern — a regular expression the whole value must match, e.g. [0-9]{6} for a PIN code.
min, max, step — bounds and allowed jumps for numbers, ranges and dates.
autocomplete — on, off, or a token such as email that lets the browser fill saved values.

blocks.text: The browser checks these before submitting: an empty required field, a malformed email, a pattern mismatch or an out-of-range number stops the send and shows a bubble on the offending field. CSS can style it with :invalid, and novalidate on the form switches the check off. This is a courtesy to the user, not a security control; the server must check again (see Unit 4, Form processing with GET and POST).

figure.caption: The browser walks the named controls in order and builds the query string for a GET form. The select contributes lang=en and the submit button contributes nothing, because it has no name.

spec.title: Submitting a search form with GET
spec.aria: A form with action /search and method get holds a text input named q and a select named lang; pressing the submit button builds the URL /search?q=html&lang=en.

examples.question: A search form has action="/search" and method="get". Inside it sit a text input with name="q" holding the typed text html, a select with name="lang" whose selected option has value="en" and the visible text English, and a submit button with no name. The user clicks the button. Write the exact URL the browser requests, and state where in the HTTP request it appears.
steps: Read the two attributes: action="/search" gives the path, method="get" says the pairs go into the URL.
Walk the controls in document order. First the text input: its name is q, its current value is html, so the pair is q=html.
Next the select: its name is lang, the selected option's value is en, so the pair is lang=en.
The submit button has no name, so it adds no pair.
Join the pairs with & and place ? between the path and the first pair: /search?q=html&lang=en.
The browser sends this as the request line GET /search?q=html&lang=en HTTP/1.1; the server reads the pairs from the query string.
examples.answer: The browser requests /search?q=html&lang=en, with both pairs carried in the URL query string.

code.code:
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input type="text" name="q" value="html">
  <select name="lang">
    <option value="en" selected>English</option>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

traps: No name, no data. A control without a name is invisible to the submission, so the server receives nothing even though the user typed.
Radio group: one shared name, different values. Different names create independent groups and let the user tick several at once.
disabled versus readonly. A disabled control is greyed out and not submitted; a readonly control is shown, not editable, and is submitted.
placeholder is a hint, not a value. An untouched field sends its value attribute (often empty), never the placeholder text.
textarea takes its starting text between its tags; a value attribute on it does nothing.

quiz.q: What does the action attribute of a form hold?
quiz.a: The URL of the server program that receives the submitted name=value pairs.

quiz.q: Why does a text input without a name send nothing?
quiz.a: The submission builds pairs from the name attribute; with no name there is no key to pair the typed value with, so the browser drops it.

quiz.q: A form has action="/find" and method="get". It holds a text input with name="q" and value="css", plus a checked checkbox with name="tags" and value="html". Write the URL requested.
quiz.a: Collect q=css, then tags=html in document order, join with & and put ? after the path: /find?q=css&tags=html.

quiz.q: A student writes method="post" on a login form, yet the password shows in the address bar. Give two likely causes.
quiz.a: The attribute was written on an inner input instead of the form, or the form actually submits through a plain link or hand-built URL. Either way the browser falls back to its default get, which places pairs in the URL.

quiz.q: Of disabled and readonly, which one still sends the field's value?
quiz.a: readonly sends the value; disabled removes the control from the submission entirely.
select restricts the user to the listed options; datalist only suggests values, and any typed text is accepted and sent.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same name/value model sits under the Constraint Validation API — checkValidity() and setCustomValidity() — and the FormData object, which serialises a form into pairs for a fetch request (Unit 3). Front-end frameworks replace the DOM's pairs with component state: a React controlled input keeps its value in state and updates it on every keystroke (Unit 5). Accessibility work ties every control to a label and wraps radio groups in a fieldset. Search for the Constraint Validation API, FormData, and React controlled components.
